name: Mind-reading machine
definition: A machine that reads a person's specific thoughts, memories or images directly from their brain.

milestones2.what: ATR labs in Kyoto reconstructed 10x10-pixel images a person viewed from brain signals.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: allowed researchers to reconstruct images from brain signals at a resolution of 10×10 pixels

milestones2.note: Only seen images are decoded, not specific thoughts or memories, so it is a partial fit; Nishimoto 2011 movie reconstruction is later. Yang Dan 1999 decoded images from cat thalamus (animal, rejected).
milestones2.check_note: Earlier decoding of seen orientations (Kamitani and Tong 2005) decodes simple features, not images; Yang Dan 1999 cat thalamus is animal. Partial fit (seen images, not thoughts), but nothing earlier fits better.

doubt: 2008 ATR reconstruction of 10x10-pixel images a person sees is a stretch: it reconstructs what was seen, not specific thoughts or memories. Carries #8, #12, #15.

name: Thought-to-text and thought display
definition: A machine that writes down a person's thoughts as text, or shows their mental images or dreams on a screen.

milestones2.what: Chang and Makin at UCSF decoded spoken sentences from ECoG signals into text with 3% word error rate.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Edward Chang and Joseph Makin from UCSF reported that ECoG signals could be used to decode speech from epilepsy patients

milestones2.note: Decodes overt speech from a 50-sentence set, not private thoughts; Willett et al. 2021 (attempted handwriting to text) is later and could not be quoted. P300 speller (1988) selects letters by attention, not thoughts. Poor fit overall.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier brain-to-letter systems (P300 speller 1988, Birbaumer slow-cortical-potential spelling 1999) select letters by attention or self-regulation, not by decoding thoughts, so rejected. Poor fit overall but the earliest brain-to-text decoding of language found.

doubt: The concept list expected this never to come true. 2020 UCSF decoding of attempted speech is not displaying thoughts: both a stretch and #1.

name: Central computer directing many robots
definition: A single computer or master robot that coordinates and directs a whole population of robots.

milestones2.what: Walgreens installed a Kiva mobile-robot fulfilment system at Mount Vernon, Illinois

sources.title: Amazon Robotics
sources.quote: Walgreens installed one at its distribution center in Mount Vernon, Illinois, in 2007

milestones2.note: Too late probably: AGV fleets under central computer traffic control existed in the 1970s (Volvo Kalmar 1972-74 seen only in search summaries, central control not confirmed). Staples 2006 not confirmed.
milestones2.check_note: Possibly too late: wire-guided AGV fleets (Volvo Kalmar 1972-74, Tetra Pak Lund 1976 with 20 AGVs and a control system per Wikipedia NDC) existed earlier, but no fetchable source states a central computer directing them, so not substituted. Staples 2006 not confirmed.

doubt: 2007 Walgreens/Kiva is one year later than the first pass's 2006 Staples/Kiva and carries four of the top 20. Centrally dispatched AGV fleets in factories and warehouses date from the 1970s-80s, but the checker found no fetchable source.

name: Brain-computer interface
definition: A link from the brain's electrical signals to a machine, so that a person controls devices by thought alone.

milestones2.what: Alvin Lucier's Music for Solo Performer (1965) used a performer's EEG alpha waves, via amplifiers and filters, to drive percussion instruments.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: one of the earliest examples of a working brain–machine interface was the piece Music for Solo Performer (1965) by American composer Alvin Lucier.

milestones2.note: Wikipedia calls it a working brain-machine interface 12 years before Vidal's 1977 EEG cursor/maze demonstration (the original). It is an art piece, so the fit is arguable; Fetz 1969 monkeys and Grey Walter 1964 rejected (animal / unverified).

milestones2.what: Kennedy and Bakay implanted a locked-in patient, Johnny Ray, who learned to control a computer cursor.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Ray's implant was installed in 1998 and he lived long enough to start working with the implant, eventually learning to control a computer cursor

milestones2.note: Birbaumer's slow cortical potential spelling device for paralysed patients (1999) is nearly contemporary; earlier lab cursor control with EEG (Wolpaw 1991) was not a service for patients.
milestones2.check_note: Birbaumer's mid-1990s paralysed-patient cursor training was a lab experiment, and his spelling device is 1999; Dobelle's 1978 implant fed vision into the brain (machine to brain) and was a prototype; Dobelle's paid service is 2002. Nothing earlier found.

doubt: Stretch introduced by the earliest-event check: Lucier's EEG concert piece (1965) as a brain-computer interface.

name: Automatic dictation transcription
definition: A machine that listens to dictation and produces the written or typed text automatically.

milestones2.what: Kyoto University's Sonotype phonetic typewriter, which prints out spoken words, reached the prototype stage (reported in Electronics, 1960-61; handled 100 Japanese monosyllables in its early version).

sources.title: Phonetic Typewriter Nears Practical Use
sources.quote: Development of a phonetic typewriter—one which will print out spoken words—has progressed at Kyoto University, Japan

milestones2.note: Tangora (mid-1980s) is far too late. Earlier fit: Kyoto Sonotype phonetic typewriter, prototype by 1960-61 (article cites an Electronics report of 27 May 1960). Even earlier is probably Olson and Belar's RCA phonetic typewriter (J. Acoust. Soc. Am., Nov 1956, single talker, ~10 syllables) but I could not fetch a page to quote it, so 1961 is the earliest sourced; true date likely 1956.

milestones2.what: Dragon Dictate released as a consumer dictation product (discrete words, DOS).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1990 – Dragon Dictate, a consumer product released in 1990.

milestones2.note: First pass said 1997 NaturallySpeaking, which was the first continuous-speech product, not the first dictation product. The same Wikipedia list gives 1987 'a recognizer from Kurzweil Applied Intelligence' (Kurzweil's medical-report dictation system); the line has no detail, so I could not confirm it as dictation and kept 1990. An earlier 1987 or 1984-85 product may fit. No mass_adoption sourced: dictation by speech only became routine on smartphones in the 2010s, but no fetched source states it.
milestones2.check_note: Kurzweil 1987 recognizer (same Wikipedia list) has no detail to confirm it was dictation; Dragon Dictate 1990 kept. Looked for an earlier product and found no fetchable source. Prior: First pass said 1997 NaturallySpeaking, which was the first continuous-speech product, not the first dictation product. The same Wikipedia list gives 1987 'a recognizer from Kurzweil Applied Intelligence' (Kurzweil's medical-report dictation system); the line has no detail, so I could not confirm it as dictation and kept 1990. An earlier 1987 or 1984-85 product may fit. No mass_adoption sourced: dictation by speech only became routine on smartphones in the 2010s, but no fetched source states it.

doubt: Date the agents called approximate: 1961 (RCA's 1956 phonetic typewriter is probably earlier, but unsourced).

name: Immersive virtual reality
definition: A machine that feeds a person's senses a computer-generated world convincing enough to feel real.

milestones2.what: Ivan Sutherland and students built a computer-driven head-mounted display (Sword of Damocles) at Harvard

sources.title: The Sword of Damocles (virtual reality)
sources.quote: The system was created in 1968 by computer scientist Ivan Sutherland with the help of his students Bob Sproull

milestones2.note: Heilig's Sensorama (1962) rejected: mechanical, not computer-generated. Philco Headsight (1961) is camera-based, not a generated world. Primitive wireframe, so fit is partial.

milestones2.what: Virtuality 1000SU VR systems launched in London in 1990 and sold to corporations (Ford, IBM, Mitsubishi, Olin) before the 1991 arcade version.

sources.title: Virtuality (product)
sources.quote: The Virtuality 1000SU VR system was launched in 1990 at the Computer Graphics ’90 exhibition held at Alexandra Palace in London.

sources.title: Virtuality (product)
sources.quote: Many other systems were sold to corporations including Ford, IBM, Mitsubishi and Olin.

milestones2.note: Original 1991 arcade release was preceded by the 1990 corporate-sale product. Military helmet simulators and VPL's 1980s RB2 could be earlier but no fetched page dated a real-purpose use, so not adopted.

name: Retina and iris recognition
definition: A machine that identifies a person by scanning the patterns of the eye.

milestones2.what: EyeDentify's retinal scanner went on the market as a commercial model in 1981 (specific scanner means patented 1978), after the device concept emerged in 1975.

sources.title: Retinal scan
sources.quote: In 1978, specific means for a retinal scanner was patented, followed by a commercial model in 1981.

milestones2.note: The concept covers retina as well as iris; retina scanning predates Daugman's 1994 iris algorithms. 1981 is the first dated working (commercial) retinal scanner found; Flom and Safir's iris concept and the 1935 Simon-Goldstein retina idea had no working device. A demonstration may precede 1981 (patent 1978) but no dated demonstration found.

name: Speech recognition and voice command
definition: A machine that recognizes spoken words and carries out spoken commands, such as voice-operated doors or computers.

milestones2.what: Bell Labs' Audrey, built by Balashek, Biddulph and Davis, recognized spoken digits from a single speaker.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1952 – Bell Labs researchers, Stephen Balashek, R. Biddulph, and K. H. Davis, built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition.

sources.title: speech recognition (Q189436)
sources.quote: start time (P580): 1952

milestones2.note: Earlier candidate: Radio Rex (Elmwood Button Co., 1922), a toy dog that leaps out of its house when its name is called. Rejected: it is triggered by acoustic energy near 500 Hz (the vowel in 'Rex'), not by recognizing words, so it is a sound-triggered switch; I also could not fetch a source page for it. Other candidates: RCA 1956 Olson-Belar syllable recognizer, IBM Shoebox 1962 (16 words), all later. Voice-operated doors/locks: no earlier working example found.
milestones2.check_note: Radio Rex (1922) responds to acoustic energy, not words, so rejected; no earlier word-recognizing machine found in fetched sources. Wikidata quote not verifiable so dropped.

milestones2.what: The Apricot Portable shipped with voice-command recognition (up to 4096 words, 64 in RAM at a time).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1984 – the Apricot Portable was released with up to 4096 words support, of which only 64 could be held in RAM at a time.

milestones2.note: Wikipedia lists the Apricot Portable first under 'Practical products'. Earlier commercial use likely exists: Threshold Technology's VIP-100 (about 1972, used for factory quality-control data entry), reported by secondary sources I could not fetch. Reject 1987 Kurzweil and 1990 DragonDictate as later. Treat 1984 as an upper bound; true first use is probably early 1970s.
milestones2.check_note: Threshold Technology VIP-100 (about 1972) is credited by secondary sources as the first commercial speech recognition product, but its hosts are blocked here and no fetched page gives a quote or date, so it cannot be substituted. Apricot Portable 1984 kept as an upper bound; true first use probably earlier.

milestones2.what: Apple launched the iPhone 4S with Siri, putting spoken commands in the hands of ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

milestones2.note: The first pass gave 2011-10-04, which is the announcement; the iPhone 4S went on sale 14 October 2011. Earlier but narrower mass uses: telephone call-routing by voice (AT&T 1992), DragonDictate/NaturallySpeaking for PC users (1990s) were niche, not routine for ordinary people.
milestones2.check_note: Rechecked for earlier routine-use of voice commands: AT&T call routing 1992 and Dragon products were niche; no earlier ordinary-consumer deployment found, so confirmed. Prior: The first pass gave 2011-10-04, which is the announcement; the iPhone 4S went on sale 14 October 2011. Earlier but narrower mass uses: telephone call-routing by voice (AT&T 1992), DragonDictate/NaturallySpeaking for PC users (1990s) were niche, not routine for ordinary people.

name: Automated face recognition
definition: Cameras and computers that identify people by matching their faces against stored images.

milestones2.what: Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located facial features and measured ratios without human intervention.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: In 1970, Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located anatomical features such as the chin

milestones2.note: Bledsoe, Chan and Bisson (1964-65) needed a human to mark feature coordinates, so rejected as semi-automated; the earlier system did the matching by computer, so a looser reading would date the demonstration to 1964-65.

milestones2.what: The Bochum face-recognition system, by 1997 outperforming other systems, was sold commercially as ZN-Face to operators of airports and other busy locations.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: was sold commercially on the market as ZN-Face to operators of airports and other busy locations.

milestones2.note: Earlier than Mexico 2000. The same article says West Virginia and New Mexico DMVs were first to use automated face recognition after 1993 (search results say West Virginia from 1998), but no dated source was fetchable. 1997 comes from ZN-Face commercial sale to airports, so it is a rough date.

milestones2.what: Apple announced Face ID on the iPhone X, bringing face recognition to ordinary phone unlocking.

sources.title: Face ID
sources.quote: Apple announced Face ID alongside the iPhone X on September 12, 2017

milestones2.note: Introduction date, not a measured adoption figure.
milestones2.check_note: Introduction date, not a measured adoption figure. Earlier face-unlock phones (e.g. Android 4.0 Face Unlock, 2011) were niche and unreliable. Kept.

name: Computerized information retrieval
definition: A machine that stores very large collections of records or documents and finds the items matching a query in seconds.

milestones2.what: Lockheed completed the earliest form of Dialog under Roger K. Summit, an online interactive retrieval system

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

milestones2.note: Earlier candidate: MEDLARS (NLM, 1964), a batch computer retrieval service, not interactive 'in seconds'; also pre-computer mechanical retrieval (Goldberg's Statistical Machine, 1931) rejected as not computerized.

milestones2.what: Lockheed's interactive Dialog system (Roger Summit) was tested on NASA's STAR database at Ames in 1966, cutting searches from 14 hours to a few minutes; this became NASA RECON.

sources.title: Roger K. Summit
sources.quote: Information searches within the NASA STAR database went from taking 14 hours, plus shipping and handling, to a few minutes with Summit's Dialog system.

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

milestones2.note: Replaces MEDLINE late 1971: Dialog was online and interactive on a large NASA database in 1966 (Ames experiment, NASA contract 1966). Result time is 'a few minutes' not strictly seconds, and 1966 was an experiment before RECON (1967 award); MEDLARS 1964 was batch. Original note: Rejected earlier: MEDLARS 1964 (launched by NLM, 'first large-scale, computer-based, retrospective search service available to the general public') was a real service but batch-mode, so it does not meet 'in seconds'. Dialog commercial service started ~1972 (not sourced). If batch counts, practical use is 1964.

name: Fully automated factory or plant
definition: A factory, mine or power plant that runs and maintains itself with few or no human workers.

milestones2.what: Fanuc's robot plant near Mount Fuji runs lights-out, robots building robots, unsupervised for up to 30 days.

sources.title: Lights out (manufacturing)
sources.quote: FANUC, a Japanese robotics company, has been a lights-out factory since 2001.

milestones2.note: First pass cited a 1981 report of Fanuc unattended operation (16 hours a day); I could not verify it, so a much earlier event likely exists. Date here is the latest-source date only.
milestones2.check_note: Searched for earlier unmanned plants. Press (Christian Science Monitor 15 Apr 1981) reportedly describes Fujitsu Fanuc's Yamanashi robot plant run by robots 16 hours a day from 1981, but csmonitor.com is blocked here so the quote could not be verified; it was also not fully unmanned. Molins System 24 (1960s) unsourced and not a self-maintaining plant. Kept 2001 on the only verified source; likely too late, so a human should re-check the 1981 report.

doubt: The first pass had 1981 for Fanuc's unattended plant; only a later (2001) Wikipedia description could be quoted. Probably about 20 years late; carries #19 and #20.

name: Speech synthesis
definition: A machine that generates spoken language with an artificial voice, such as a talking computer reading out answers.

milestones2.what: Wolfgang von Kempelen's bellows-operated acoustic-mechanical speech machine, with models of tongue and lips producing vowels and consonants, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: There followed the bellows-operated "acoustic-mechanical speech machine" of Wolfgang von Kempelen of Pressburg, Hungary, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Wolfgang von Kempelen
sources.quote: Kempelen also created a manually operated speaking machine.

milestones2.note: Date is the publication of his description; he worked on the machine for about twenty years before, so a working demonstration probably came earlier (the same page gives 1789 for his book, so sources conflict). Earlier candidate: Kratzenstein 1779, vocal-tract models producing five vowels only, rejected as not producing speech. Later: Voder 1939 (first electronic, human-operated, shown at the New York World's Fair), Kelly-Gerstman IBM 7090 computer synthesis 1961, Umeda's English text-to-speech 1968. The machine was hand-operated, as was the Voder.

milestones2.what: Telesensory Systems' Speech+ talking calculator for the blind, with a synthesized voice, was in use; the Kurzweil Reading Machine for the Blind (Votrax synthesizer) appeared in the same year.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: One of the first was the Telesensory Systems Inc. (TSI) Speech+ portable calculator for the blind in 1976.

milestones2.note: Earlier systems existed (Umeda's 1968 text-to-speech, MUSA 1975 reading Italian) but I found no evidence they were used outside the lab. Voder (1939) and Kempelen's machine were exhibitions. Date 1976 is the source's year for 'one of the first' handheld devices; a slightly earlier use is possible.
milestones2.check_note: Rechecked: Votrax VS4 (1971-73), Unix speak (1972-74), MUSA 1975 were lab or commercial components with no documented end use; Kurzweil Reading Machine (Votrax-based) is the same era. 1976 confirmed on the evidence available. Prior: Earlier systems existed (Umeda's 1968 text-to-speech, MUSA 1975 reading Italian) but I found no evidence they were used outside the lab. Voder (1939) and Kempelen's machine were exhibitions. Date 1976 is the source's year for 'one of the first' handheld devices; a slightly earlier use is possible.

milestones2.what: Siri on the iPhone 4S brought a talking computer that answers aloud to ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

milestones2.note: Judgment call. Earlier mass-market talking devices: Texas Instruments Speak & Spell (1978) and talking games and chess computers (1979-80), which had voices but little routine use as 'answering computers'. Wikipedia source supports the date of launch, not the synthesis itself.
milestones2.check_note: Judgment call. Earlier mass-market talking devices: Texas Instruments Speak & Spell (1978) and talking games and chess computers (1979-80), which had voices but little routine use as 'answering computers'. Wikipedia source supports the date of launch, not the synthesis itself.

name: Robot police and security guards
definition: Robots that patrol, guard buildings, check credentials or arrest people on behalf of authorities.

milestones2.what: Knightscope shipped its first autonomous security patrol robot

sources.title: Knightscope
sources.quote: Knightscope shipped their first robot in 2015.

milestones2.note: Almost certainly too late. Earlier: Denning Sentry (mid-1980s), ROBART I (c. 1982), PROWLER armed sentry (developed from 1983); I could not fetch usable dated sources for them.
milestones2.check_note: Knightscope 2015 is probably late. Earlier: Denning Sentry, introduced 1985 per Computer History Museum ('designed this robot as a security guard patrolling for up to 14 hours'), but CHM says the product did not succeed and press said none were sold, so practical use is not shown; Cybermotion SR2 at LACMA, ROBART and PROWLER could not be dated or sourced. A human should look for first deployed Cybermotion/Denning units.

doubt: 2015 Knightscope: the checker named likely earlier security robots (1980s) but could not source them.

name: Machine-readable identity and access card
definition: A card, disc or token encoded with a person's identity that machines read to grant access or check identity.

milestones2.what: IBM developed a way of attaching magnetic stripes to plastic cards under a US government contract for a security system.

sources.title: Magnetic stripe card
sources.quote: In 1960, IBM built upon the magnetic tape idea and developed a reliable way of securing magnetic stripes to plastic cards

milestones2.note: The same article says Forrest Parry had the idea in 1969, so 1960 conflicts with it. Punched-card key systems and earlier access cards were not checked.
milestones2.check_note: IBM magnetic-stripe card 1960 under a US government security contract; conflicts with the 1969 Parry account in the same article. Earlier machine-read cards found (Charga-Plate 1928 was imprinted, not machine-read; Hollerith cards are not identity tokens; smart-card patents 1967+ and Honeywell punched-card access 1965 are later). Kept.

milestones2.what: The Rochester Institute of Technology 'VALI-DINE' system used cards with mechanically punched holes, read by machine, to let students into dining halls.

sources.title: Campus card
sources.quote: Electronic card access has been available on campuses since as early as 1968.

sources.title: Campus card
sources.quote: relied on cards with mechanically punched holes to allow access to their dining halls.

milestones2.note: Replaces 1975 VingCard (1975 launch, first hotel install 1978). Campus card article dates RIT VALI-DINE card access to 1968, a machine-read identity/access card in real use. Search results also mention a 1965 Honeywell punched-card access system but it is unsourced. Hand-geometry Identimat (1970s) is later.

name: Companion or sex robot
definition: A robot built to provide companionship, affection, romance or sex.

milestones2.what: Sony introduced the first consumer AIBO robot dog (ERS-110)

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: The first consumer model was introduced on 11 May 1999 and was followed by updated generations.

milestones2.note: Companionship fit is loose (AIBO means pal). Paro was designed from 1993 but first shown to the public in late 2001 per the page read (first pass said 1998, not confirmed). No romance or sex robot (RealDoll 1997 is a doll, not a robot; Realbotix 2018) earlier.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier: Elektro/Sparko 1939-40 are exhibits, Paro designed from 1993 but first public in 2001, Furby 1998 is a toy creature not a companion. No earlier robot built for companionship found. Companionship fit of AIBO is loose.

milestones2.what: AIBO ERS-110 went on sale and sold out in 20 minutes

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: Sales began on 1 June 1999 and sold out via the Internet in 20 minutes.

milestones2.note: Paro handmade versions sold from 2004 are later.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier: Paro handmade sales from 2004, Furby 1998 is a pet toy, not marketed as companion robot; no earlier sale of a companion robot found.

name: Question-answering computer
definition: A computer holding broad knowledge that answers arbitrary factual questions put to it in ordinary language.

milestones2.what: MIT's START natural-language system went online on the Internet in 1993 and answered English questions on many topics (Boris Katz, MIT)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: Boris Katz is the creator of the START information processing system (since 1993 - on the Internet)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: START natural language system that allows the user to access various types of information using English

milestones2.note: START (1993) answered open-ended English questions about places, people, movies and more over the Web, an earlier broad-domain system than Watson 2011; its knowledge came from hand-annotated sources so breadth is limited (hence low). BASEBALL 1961, LUNAR 1971, SHRDLU, Unix Consultant and LILOG are narrow-domain; Ask Jeeves 1996 matched questions to web pages; Wolfram Alpha 2009 and Watson 2011 are later.

name: Machine-generated writing
definition: A computer that composes stories, articles, poems or books automatically.

milestones2.what: John Clark's Eureka, a mechanical machine that generated Latin hexameter verses automatically (about one a minute), was exhibited at the Egyptian Hall, London, after being built 1830-1845.

sources.title: The Eureka
sources.quote: named John Clark, who then exhibited his invention in the Egyptian Hall in London.

milestones2.note: Mechanical, not a computer; it fits 'composes poems automatically' but a strict reading of 'a computer' would give Christopher Strachey's love-letter generator on the Ferranti Mark 1 / Manchester Mark 1 (1952), the first computer-generated literature, which is the first pass candidate (the first pass said 1953; sources give summer 1952, one gives 1953). Eureka's method was the published 1677 scheme of John Peter, but Clark fully automated it. Build dates: 1830-1843 (some sources) or 1845. Shannon's 1948 Markov text examples were hand-made and not considered.

milestones2.what: Environment Canada deployed FoG, which generated weather forecasts in English and French from data automatically.

sources.title: Natural-language generation
sources.quote: The earliest such system to be deployed was FoG, which was used by Environment Canada to generate weather forecasts

milestones2.note: Source says only 'early 1990s'; 1990 is a placeholder year. Literature I recall gives about 1992 but I did not source it. Later: Reuters Tracer and the Associated Press / Los Angeles Times Quakebot (2014). Earlier practical text generation (e.g. form-letter mail merge) is a template fill, not composition. Eureka (1845) was a paid exhibition, not a practical tool.
milestones2.check_note: Source says only 'early 1990s'; 1990 is a placeholder year. Literature I recall gives about 1992 but I did not source it. Later: Reuters Tracer and the Associated Press / Los Angeles Times Quakebot (2014). Earlier practical text generation (e.g. form-letter mail merge) is a template fill, not composition. Eureka (1845) was a paid exhibition, not a practical tool.

milestones2.what: ChatGPT made automatic writing of text available to ordinary users, reaching 100 million users in two months.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

milestones2.note: Earlier mass exposure was to machine-written news snippets (AP earnings and sports reports since 2014) that readers did not choose or operate; ChatGPT is when ordinary people used machine writing routinely themselves.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier mass exposure was to machine-written news snippets (AP earnings and sports reports since 2014) that readers did not choose or operate; ChatGPT is when ordinary people used machine writing routinely themselves.

name: Three-dimensional holographic display
definition: A display that shows images, maps or people as volumetric three-dimensional pictures viewable from several sides.

milestones2.what: First practical optical holograms recording 3D objects made by Denisyuk (USSR) and by Leith and Upatnieks (Michigan), viewable from several angles

sources.title: Holography
sources.quote: the first practical optical holograms that recorded 3D objects to be made in 1962 by Yuri Denisyuk in the Soviet Union

milestones2.note: Static holograms are a loose match for a 'display'. Other candidates: 1966 varifocal-mirror volumetric display (Volumetric display page), 1972 moving white-light hologram (Lloyd Cross), 1989 MIT electroholographic video display. Perspecta (2001) rejected as late. Gabor 1947-48 holography produced no 3D display.

milestones2.what: Lloyd Cross produced a hologram recreating a moving 3-dimensional image (Multiplex hologram, viewable around a cylinder)

sources.title: Holographic display
sources.quote: 1972 - Lloyd Cross produced the first traditional hologram by using white-light transmission holography to recreate a moving 3-dimensional image.

milestones2.note: 1989 MIT electroholography is a lab system, not practical use. The 1972 Cross moving-image hologram is the earliest fetched 3D hologram display shown to the public (holography art exhibitions from 1968, per Wikipedia Holography, are static plates). Judgement call: practical use is thin, so low.

doubt: Stretch: static holograms (1962) as a 3D display.

name: Touchscreen and gesture interface
definition: Controlling a machine by touching a screen or panel, or by hand gestures and gloves read by sensors.

milestones2.what: E. A. Johnson (Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern) published a finger-driven capacitive touchscreen for air traffic control

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: He described his work on capacitive touchscreens in a short article published in 1965

milestones2.note: Earlier: AT&T Harmon 1962 patent for a light-beam stylus touchscreen (patent only, not shown working). Data gloves: Sayre Glove 1977, later. Light pens (1950s) are pointing devices, not touch.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier: Philco 1946 stylus patent (overlay on TV, not touch input), AT&T Harmon 1962 light-beam patent (patent only, no working system shown), Graham 1963 light-pen patent. Johnson 1965 is the first finger-driven touchscreen per Wikipedia. Gesture side: nothing earlier controlling a machine fits (theremin is a musical instrument, not machine control).

milestones2.what: PLATO IV terminals, introduced at the University of Illinois in 1972, had a built-in 16x16 infrared touch panel students used to answer questions

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: In 1972, with the introduction of PLATO IV, Bitzer declared general success

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: Touch panel: A 16×16 grid infrared touch panel, allowing students to answer questions by touching anywhere on the screen.

milestones2.note: CERN's touchscreen was put to use in 1973; PLATO IV touch panels were part of the 1972 classroom system (Wikipedia Touchscreen dates the optical patent filing to 1972). Johnson's ATC touchscreen and the 1970 Telefunken device were described in the 1960s-70 but no fetched source gives deployed use earlier.

milestones2.what: Touchscreen phones were rapidly gaining popularity by 2009 after the 2007 LG Prada and iPhone

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: By 2009, touchscreen-enabled phones were rapidly gaining popularity

milestones2.note: Date is a judgement (2007-2010). iPhone announced Jan 2007; first-pass 2007 date replaced by when popularity is stated.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier touchscreens in ATMs, kiosks, HP-150 (1983), IBM Simon (1993), Nintendo DS (2004) were niche or early-stage, not routine use by ordinary people; 2009 majority of smartphones shipping with touchscreens (Wikipedia) supports 2007-2009 as the mass-adoption window.

name: Computer screen display
definition: A screen on which a computer shows text, graphics or data to its user, in place of printouts or dials.

milestones2.what: Manchester Baby (SSEM) had an output CRT displaying the bit pattern of its stores, from which results were read (working June 1948)

sources.title: Manchester Baby
sources.quote: was used as the output device, able to display the bit pattern of any selected storage tube

milestones2.note: Whirlwind 1949 is a later display of a computed solution; the Baby's fourth CRT was dedicated output showing the machine's data to its operator, which fits 'screen shows data to its user' though only as bit patterns (hence low). EDSAC/Mark 1 CRTs are 1949 or later.

milestones2.what: Whirlwind became operational in 1951, real-time output on CRT displays used in Cape Cod radar tracking

sources.title: Whirlwind I
sources.quote: Operational in 1951, it was among the first digital electronic computers that operated in real-time for output

milestones2.note: Display-specific operational use date is approximate; SAGE-like display uses (1951 Bedford test) are the same era.
milestones2.check_note: Looked for earlier practical use of screens: Manchester Baby 1948 and Williams tubes were demonstration/engineering. SAGE and the Cape Cod system displays are same era or later. Date kept as an approximation.

name: Machine learning
definition: A machine that improves its performance from experience or data instead of being explicitly programmed for each task.

milestones2.what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC at Princeton (funding summer 1951), a neural-net machine that learned by reinforcement to solve a maze.

sources.title: Stochastic neural analog reinforcement calculator
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

milestones2.note: Candidates: Ashby's Homeostat (1948, adapts to disturbances; closer to self-regulation than learning from experience), Shannon's Theseus maze mouse (1950; relays remember the maze path, and whether it 'learned' is disputed), Samuel's checkers program (begun 1949, first ran 1952, paper 1959; 'machine learning' coined 1959) and Rosenblatt's perceptron (1957-58). SNARC is a simulated maze solved by reinforced weights, so I take it as the earliest clear case, but this is a judgment and the date is only the year. Page for Theseus could not be fetched. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: ADALINE (1960) adaptive filters and later uses were not sourced, and 'routine' consumer use is too diffuse to date.

name: Robot vacuum cleaner and lawn mower
definition: A small autonomous machine that cleans floors or mows a lawn on its own.

milestones2.what: Whirlpool demonstrated a track-following robotic floor sweeper concept (Donald Moore's 1957 patent) at the American National Exhibition in Moscow

sources.title: Robotic vacuum cleaner
sources.quote: Whirlpool demonstrated the concept at the 1959 American National Exhibition but did not bring it to market.

milestones2.note: Follows a track under the floor, so only a loose fit to 'on its own'. Later: MowBot 1969, Electrolux Trilobite 1996, Roomba 2002. Heinlein 1956 was fiction.

milestones2.what: MowBot, autonomous robotic lawn mower patented by S. Lawrence Bellinger, sold for about $800

sources.title: Robotic lawn mower
sources.quote: In 1969, the MowBot was introduced and patented by S Lawrence Bellinger having many features of today's most popular products.

milestones2.note: No earlier robot mower or vacuum on sale found in the pages read. Trilobite (1996) and Roomba (2002) are later. Whether MowBot was truly autonomous rests on this one source.

name: Electronic book reader
definition: A portable screen device that displays the text of books and documents stored electronically in place of paper.

milestones2.what: George Yevick and Adnan Wally invented an e-reader with a liquid-crystal display

sources.title: E-reader
sources.quote: The first e-reader was invented by George Yevick and Adnan Wally in 1972.

milestones2.note: Source says invented and never commercialized; unclear whether a working unit was built. Dynabook (Kay, 1968-72) was a concept only.

milestones2.what: Sony Data Discman DD-1, a handheld electronic book player reading books on mini-CD, sold in Japan in 1990

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: The DD-1 was the earlier Japanese model in 1990.

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: is an electronic book player developed and marketed by Sony Corporation

milestones2.note: Earlier than Rocket eBook 1998; Wikipedia's E-reader article lists the Data Discman among the first commercial e-readers. Later Western release 1991/92. Pre-1990 portable electronic book devices (e.g. Franklin dictionaries, Sony 1980s) not found in a fetched source.

name: 3D printing
definition: A machine that builds solid objects automatically from a digital design by adding material layer by layer.

milestones2.what: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute) published methods and results for building 3D plastic models layer by layer from photo-hardening polymer.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: His research results as journal papers were published in April and November 1981.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: In April 1980, Hideo Kodama of Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute invented two additive methods for fabricating three-dimensional plastic models

milestones2.note: Earlier than Hull's 1984 patent. Raytheon 1982 layered-powder patent is later. Whether Kodama's design was driven by a digital design file is not stated; fit is on layer-by-layer automatic building.

milestones2.what: 3D Systems, co-founded by Chuck Hull, commercialised stereolithography (first machine, SLA-1, reported 1987).

sources.title: Stereolithography
sources.quote: After the patent was granted in 1986, Hull co-founded the world's first 3D printing company, 3D Systems, to commercialize it.

milestones2.note: Quote supports commercialisation after 1986 only; the 1987 SLA-1 date comes from the first pass and was not fetched. No mass_adoption established (consumer RepRap era 2005+ not sourced as routine use).

name: Real-time computerized situation display
definition: A computer-driven screen or plotting board that shows the live positions of ships, aircraft or objects tracked by radar and sensors.

milestones2.what: Bedford, MA test: radar data sent by phone line to a computer, displaying a mock enemy aircraft detection (Whirlwind)

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: data produced by a radar was transmitted through telephone lines to a computer for the first time, showing the detection of a mock enemy aircraft.

milestones2.note: Other candidates: DATAR (Royal Canadian Navy/Ferranti, trial late 1953 on Lake Ontario, displays on plan-position indicators), Cape Cod System tests from Sept 1953, Royal Navy CDS (analog, 1940s). 1951 is earliest found.

milestones2.what: SAGE New York sector became operational, direction-center consoles showing radar tracks from the computer

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: On "June 26, 1958,…the New York sector became operational"

milestones2.note: First pass said 1958-07-01 at McGuire AFB; fetched page gives 26 June 1958 for New York sector. DATAR was not fielded; CDS-based Royal Navy ADA later.

name: Neural implant and cyborg augmentation
definition: An electronic device implanted in or joined to the human body or brain to restore or extend senses, memory or ability.

milestones2.what: Djourno and Eyries in France invented the original cochlear implant, stimulating the auditory nerve electrically.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: André Djourno and Charles Eyriès invented the original cochlear implant in 1957.

milestones2.note: Earlier than the first-pass House 1961. Cardiac pacemaker implants (1958) are body implants not neural/sensory, so rejected for this concept.

milestones2.what: Hochmair's multichannel cochlear implant was first implanted in a person in Vienna, followed by Clark's in 1978; both were commercialized.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: with the Hochmairs' device first implanted in a person in December 1977 and Clark's in August 1978

milestones2.note: House/3M single-channel devices were marketed from 1972 and FDA-approved for adults in 1984 (not verified with a fetched quote), which may be earlier practical use. Date here is a weak proxy.

name: Spacecraft guidance and navigation computer
definition: A computer that calculates orbits, courses and engine burns and steers a spacecraft or ship along them.

milestones2.what: Gemini 3 flew with the IBM Gemini guidance computer, controlling mission maneuvers (orbit changes by crew).

sources.title: Gemini Guidance Computer
sources.quote: The computer, which facilitated the control of mission maneuvers, was designed by the IBM Federal Systems Division.

sources.title: Gemini 3
sources.quote: It was the first U.S. mission in which the crew fired thrusters to change the size and shape of their orbit

milestones2.note: Earlier than the first pass (Apollo 1968). That Gemini 3 carried the computer is from background knowledge, not a fetched sentence. Missile and submarine inertial guidance computers (late 1950s) not checked.

milestones2.what: Same flight: first operational use of an onboard computer for orbital maneuvers on a crewed spacecraft.

sources.title: Gemini Guidance Computer
sources.quote: The computer, which facilitated the control of mission maneuvers, was designed by the IBM Federal Systems Division.

milestones2.note: Same event as the demonstration; see note there.

name: Computer-run space station
definition: A computer that runs the life support, systems and operations of a space station or colony.

milestones2.what: Skylab launched with an onboard digital computer controlling its attitude and pointing.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: The mission computer used aboard Skylab was the IBM System/4Pi TC-1, a relative of the AP-101 Space Shuttle computers.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: Skylab was launched on May 14, 1973, by the modified Saturn V.

milestones2.note: Sources show an onboard computer for attitude control only, not life support. Salyut 1 (1971) computers not found in fetchable sources, so an earlier event may exist.

definition: A robot that serves customers or the public as a waiter, bartender, clerk, receptionist or guide.
